content: The umbilical vein is a vital blood vessel present during fetal development. It is responsible for transporting oxygenated blood from the placenta to the developing fetus. The placenta, which is attached to the uterine lining, serves as the site of gas exchange between the mother and the fetus. The umbilical cord contains three vessels: a single umbilical vein and two umbilical arteries. The umbilical vein carries oxygenated blood from the placenta to the fetus, while the two umbilical arteries return deoxygenated blood from the fetus to the placenta. These vessels are coiled together within a protective substance called Wharton’s jelly and enter the fetal abdomen at the umbilicus. Once inside the fetus, the umbilical vein travels alongside the falciform ligament and reaches the underside of the liver. At the transverse fissure of the liver, the umbilical vein divides into two branches: one larger and one smaller. The larger branch joins the portal vein and together they enter the right lobe of the liver. The smaller branch, known as the ductus venosus, bypasses the liver and connects directly to the inferior vena cava, allowing oxygenated blood to flow toward the fetal heart. Within approximately one week after birth, the umbilical vein undergoes complete obliteration and is replaced by a fibrous cord called the round ligament of the liver (ligamentum teres hepatis). This structure extends from the umbilicus to the transverse fissure of the liver, where it joins the ligamentum venosum, which separates the left and right lobes of the liver. The closure of the umbilical vein typically occurs after the umbilical arteries have closed. This delayed closure allows for continued communication between the placenta and the fetal heart, facilitating an autotransfusion of remaining blood from the placenta to the newborn. In certain pathological conditions, such as cirrhosis and portal hypertension, the round ligament may reopen under extreme pressure to allow blood flow. This process, known as recanalization, is common in patients with cirrhosis. In cirrhosis, rapid scar tissue formation in and around the liver can obstruct nearby blood vessels, increasing vascular resistance and leading to portal hypertension. The abnormally high blood pressure in the vessels surrounding the liver can exert enough force to reopen the round ligament, allowing blood to bypass the liver. In newborns, the umbilical vein remains patent for at least a few months after birth. During this time, it can be catheterized to provide intravenous access. This is particularly useful for administering regular transfusions in cases of erythroblastosis fetalis or hemolytic disease of the newborn. Illustrations and diagrams of placental circulation, vascular channels in early human embryos, and the anatomy of the liver and embryonic structures provide further insight into the development and function of the umbilical vein and its associated structures.
